canonical_statement: The paper aims to generalize the original F(AI)2R provenance model beyond scholarly writing into a domain-agnostic PROV-O extension named aiprov.
The paper aims to package the provenance method as an executable skill that an AI agent can operate on its own work.
The paper uses its own production process as a self-applied meta-experiment in which the provenance graph is the evaluation object.
The paper identifies three contributions: aiprov, an executable-skill implementation, and a self-applied meta-experiment.
aiprov extends PROV-O with HumanAgent, AIAgent, and ToolAgent classes; AuthoringPass, AuditPass, Build, and Repair activities; and entities for artefacts, claims, sources, transcripts, and prompts.
Prompts are treated as executable plans bound to AI activities, while transcripts are retained so auditors can inspect the instructions and dialogue that shaped an artefact.
Activities may record request/session identifiers, token classes, sampling parameters, cost, energy, and tools, under an omit-don’t-estimate rule for unavailable telemetry.
Generated artefacts receive SHA-256 content hashes at logging time, and prompt files receive prompt hashes.
Invariant I requires every claim to have a generating activity, an attributed agent, and a verification state, with violations treated as hard conformance failures.
Invariant II implements a verification ladder whose promotions must strictly increase and are themselves logged as audit activities with a grantor.
Verification rungs 5 (human-confirmed) and 6 (human-read) are restricted to human agents; an AI-granted promotion to either rung is a hard validator failure.
The source-vendored rung is an access gate for human verification rather than an evidential claim; tooling requires a vendored copy or clear access link before human-only promotions.
Commit binding uses a two-commit pattern: commit artefacts first, log an activity that binds that commit, then commit the graph update separately.

The conformance validator comprises seven SPARQL checks; four are hard failures with a nonzero exit code and the remainder include warnings for conditions such as agentless activities or mutable link-only human audit targets.
The tooling includes report aggregation, backward-closure extraction, and a self-contained provenance dashboard.
Source registration searches open bibliographic registries and only promotes a source to reference-resolved when its DOI or URL actually resolves and metadata are captured.
Skill setup asks the human operator for an ORCID iD, resolves available registry identity data without guessing, derives the instance base from the git remote, and scaffolds CI and a paper skeleton.
Every push runs server-side graph validation, dashboard rendering, disclosure regeneration, and PDF compilation; conformance failure blocks the build.
The skill can republish a live preview and a source-verification queue; human grant or refusal actions can be staged through authenticated repository issues and transcribed into the graph.
The authoring workflow separates structure from prose by creating reviewable section skeletons before prose generation, with both passes logged.
The AI-transparency statement is derived from the provenance graph on every build rather than maintained as a separate manual disclosure.
The experimental-data example in Section V is explicitly presented as a prospective design rather than an implemented deployment.
An auditor is expected to clone the repository and independently rerun validation, re-hash vendored or committed artefacts, re-resolve DOIs, and inspect activity and transcript records.
A distributed reviewer library, backward-closure propagation, and dispute-routing workflow are described as designed extensions rather than shipped features.
The evaluation is a demonstration rather than a comparative study: one human operator, one AI system, one CI tool agent, one working session, and one paper/domain.

canonical_statement: The provenance graph is only as truthful as its writer; content hashes, commit binding, CI validation, and human-only rungs mitigate but do not eliminate self-report dishonesty.

Provider-signed inference records could reduce agent under-reporting but would shift trust to provider key custody, stop at the API seam, and still could not prove that a human read carefully or judged correctly.
The paper proposes a dual-witness direction in which provider-signed inference logs and repository-side commit binding cross-reference each other, optionally anchored by a third append-only witness.
The human-only verification rungs record attributable human judgement, not machine-verifiable correctness of that judgement.
Energy consumption was not recorded because the provider did not report energy telemetry; the schema reserves an energy field but it remained empty.

The paper does not determine whether the reported computational consumption and environmental cost are justified; it argues only that such judgements should be based on recorded rather than guessed consumption.
The skill evolved from v0 to v0.21 during the experiment, including two operator-contested ladder redesigns, while archived snapshots and commit binding retained method-version attribution.
The transparency disclosure states that Claude Code was associated with 206 recorded activities.

canonical_statement: Table III’s reported AI activity counts (67 authoring + 163 audit + 12 repair) sum to 242, which does not reconcile with the transparency statement’s 206 Claude Code-associated activities without additional explanation.

The ai-confirmed source judgements were made by the same agent that wrote the citing sentences, leaving self-confirmation bias unmeasured; the paper calls for independent model or sampled-human re-verification.
The meta-experiment is a single self-applied case; portability claims require application by a second operator in a second domain and comparison of the records.
The paper explicitly states that the method does not settle what science with AI in the loop should become and is intended as technical support while norms remain contested.
The paper raises the possibility that instrumenting PDF production may target a legacy artefact, while arguing that the graph-level invariants can survive if narrative papers become derived views.

The authors conclude that aiprov generalizes F(AI)2R into a domain-agnostic PROV-O extension, packages it as an executable skill, and demonstrates self-application with versioned provenance of both successes and mishaps.
The paper frames the principal value of fast AI-assisted work as auditability rather than speed: provenance should distinguish rapid, traceable work from rapid noise.

The skill bundle, provenance graph, transcripts, and paper sources are reported as public in the project repository, and the demonstration data are archived on Zenodo under DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21667684.

Future work named by the paper includes multi-agent attribution, energy accounting, broader registry integration, default source vendoring, integration with uncertainty-aware provenance, permanent vocabulary registration, independent re-verification, and cross-operator/domain replication.
